title: Crime & Punishment: Application
welcome_lead: Now apply the teachings: forgiveness, the death penalty, and what Christianity and Islam say about specific responses to crime.
meta_desc: GCSE RS Crime & Punishment application — forgiveness, capital punishment, Christian and Muslim teachings.
final_note: You can now compare Christian and Muslim teachings on punishment and forgiveness.

concepts.def: Deterrence, retribution, reformation, protection, reparation; Christianity emphasises reformation; modern justice mixes aims.
Death penalty; Christians divided (Catholics now oppose); Sharia permits for murder; abolished in UK 1965.
Victim-offender dialogue and reparation; mirrors Christian forgiveness and Jewish teshuvah (return).
Offences motivated by prejudice against identity; Sentencing Act 2020 enhanced penalties; religions condemn.
'Eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24); originally limited excessive revenge; Jesus reinterpreted (Matthew 5:38).
Christianity Matthew 18:22 'seventy times seven'; Islam Qur'an 24:22; central to dealing with crime.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Jesus taught radical forgiveness — 'seventy-seven times' (Matthew 18:22).

The Lord's Prayer: 'Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us' (Matthew 6:12).

The Qur'an says 'Repel evil with what is better' (41:34) and praises those who pardon others.

The UK abolished the death penalty for murder in 1965 (completely 1998). The Roman Catholic Church now teaches the death penalty is 'inadmissible' (Catechism, updated 2018).

Some Christians point to Genesis 9:6 to support it. In Islamic teaching, qisas (retaliation) is permitted for murder but the family can forgive (Qur'an 2:178).

Restorative justice brings offender and victim together to repair harm. Many Christians see this as embodying gospel values of forgiveness and reconciliation.

Community service, prison and fines are common UK responses. Reformation programmes (education, therapy) reflect a Christian and Islamic concern for redemption.
